Cross-validation workflow for the group project

Author

Shew Fan Liu

Published

October 1, 2026

All decisions are made on the training set. The test set is used once, at the end. Each box names the Lesson 7 section that teaches it.

How this relates to Lesson 7

Lesson 7 runs CV on the full Auto data, because its job is to teach the mechanics of CV. Its summary workflow has three steps: CV, select, refit. Your project adds two things around that core:

  • A test set split off first (step 1). CV chooses the model. The winner’s CV score is optimistic, because choosing the lowest of several noisy estimates favours the one that came out low by chance. The test set gives an estimate that played no part in the choice.
  • A single audit (step 7). The test set is scored once, for the winner only.

Steps 3 to 6 and step 8 are exactly what Lesson 7 teaches. Run them on the training set instead of the full data.

The steps

  1. Check data quality, then split once. Before splitting, check the shape, the outcome type, missing-value markers such as '?', duplicate rows and class balance. These checks look only at data quality, not at how predictors relate to the outcome. Then use train_test_split with random_state=2026 (Lesson 7,.4), and add stratify=y for a binary outcome (7.7). Every observation you hold out is one fewer for building and selecting the model. Keep this in mind when selecting the split size. The test set is not called until the very end. It is used once, after the model is fixed, as a final audit before the model is deployed. Lock it away at this point.

  2. EDA on the training set. Look at predictor distributions, relationships with the outcome and candidate transformations using the training set only. What you learn here shapes the model, so it must not come from the test set.

  3. Build a Pipeline. Put every preprocessing step that learns from data (scaling, encoding, imputation) inside the Pipeline with the model (Lesson 7.8). Each fold then learns its own means and SDs, so nothing leaks from the validation fold. Steps that do not learn from the validation set such as taking a log, can stay outside the pipeline.

  4. Set folds and metric. Use KFold for regression (7.6) and StratifiedKFold for classification (7.7), with k = 5 or 10, shuffle=True and a fixed random_state. Choose the metric before you look at results, using the scoring strings in 7.5 and 7.7. Use MSE for regression. For classification use AUC, or sensitivity if false negatives cost more.

  5. Cross-validate every candidate. Run each model family through the same splitter with cross_val_score (7.6.1). Use GridSearchCV (Lesson 9) when a model has a tuning parameter (λ, degree, subset size). Use the same folds for every candidate so the comparison is fair. Record each candidate model’s CV error as the mean of its k fold errors, with SE = SD of the fold errors / k\sqrt k.

  6. Select one winner and refit it on the training set. Report the mean and SE of the CV error across folds. Choose the lowest mean, or the simplest model within one SE of it (the one-SE rule, Lesson 8). Lesson 7.6.1, does this by eye on the Auto CV curve. Fit the winner once on the full training set, all folds combined. This is the same refit as Lesson 7.6.2, applied to the training set (not to all the data). GridSearchCV does this step for you via best_estimator_ which is already refit on the full training set (Lesson 9). The model is now fixed.

  7. Score on test, once. Evaluate the step 6 model on the test set. Do not refit it. This is the final audit of how well the model generalises. Scoring a second model on the test set turns it into another validation set.

  8. Refit on all data. Refit the winner’s exact specification on train and test combined to get the final model (Lesson 7.6.2). sklearn handles prediction and CV but returns no SEs or p-values. For coefficient tables and CIs, refit the same specification in statsmodels. Keep the step 7 score as the performance figure you report.

The procedure, for each candidate model:

  1. Fit on four folds and compute the MSE on the held-out fold. Repeat for all five splits. This gives five validation MSEs.

  2. CV error = the mean of the five.

  3. SE = SD of the five / 5\sqrt 5.

Run this for every candidate on the same five folds, then pick the winner:

  • Lowest mean: take the candidate with the smallest CV error.

  • One-SE rule: take the minimum CV error and add its SE to get a threshold. Pick the simplest candidate whose CV error falls below the threshold.

Did the audit pass?

Set the pass criteria before you score the test set, the same way you fix the metric in step 4.

The audit passes when both hold:

  • The test score agrees with CV. It falls within the spread of the fold scores, roughly the CV mean ±2SE\pm\, 2\,\text{SE}. CV predicted this number. The test set checks the prediction.

  • The model beats a baseline.

    • Regression. Predict the training mean for every test observation and compute the baseline MSE. Compare it to the test MSE of the winning model. Your model’s test MSE must be clearly lower.

      MSEbaseline=1ntest∑i∈test(yi−y‾train)2MSEmodel=1ntest∑i∈test(yi−ŷi)2 \begin{aligned} \text{MSE}_{\text{baseline}} &= \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \left( y_i - \bar{y}_{\text{train}} \right)^2 \\ \text{MSE}_{\text{model}} &= \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2 \end{aligned}

    • Classification. Predict the majority class of the training set for every test observation and compute the baseline accuracy. Compare it to the test accuracy of the winning model. Your model’s test accuracy must be clearly higher. If AUC is your metric, the baseline is 0.5, because a model that gives every observation the same prediction cannot rank anyone.

      Accbaseline=1ntest∑i∈test𝟏(yi=ctrain)Accmodel=1ntest∑i∈test𝟏(yi=ŷi) \begin{aligned} \text{Acc}_{\text{baseline}} &= \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \mathbf{1}\left( y_i = c_{\text{train}} \right) \\ \text{Acc}_{\text{model}} &= \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \mathbf{1}\left( y_i = \hat{y}_i \right) \end{aligned}

      Here ctrainc_{\text{train}} is the majority class in the training set, and 𝟏(⋅)\mathbf{1}(\cdot) equals 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise.

If both hold, go to step 8. Refit only the coefficients. Predictors, preprocessing, model family and tuned hyperparameters stay frozen. Re-selecting on the full data deploys a model you never audited.

The audit fails when either breaks:

  • Test error well above the CV range. Common causes:
    • leakage inside the CV loop (Lesson 7.8);
    • a split that does not represent the data, such as a time ordering or cluster structure;
    • overfitting to CV after comparing many candidates.
  • Test error well below the CV range. Investigate this too. It usually means a lucky or unrepresentative split.
  • No better than the baseline. The model has learned nothing useful, whatever CV said.

After a failure, the test set is spent. Do not fix the model and score the same test set again. That turns it into a validation set, and the new score is no longer an audit. Diagnose the cause and report the failed audit. Describe the corrections you would make to the training process. The revised model needs a fresh holdout before it can be audited.

Choosing the test set size. Larger test sets give a stabler audit but leave less data for selection. 20% to 30% is a common default. Hold out less when data are scarce, but keep enough test cases, and for classification enough minority-class cases, that a few observations cannot swing the score.
